intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit two: the law of treaties. This is the longest unit in the course, and it is built around twelve questions you ask of any treaty. Keep that list in your head as we go — it is also the best case-solving checklist you will get.

slides.2: The unit opens by re-anchoring treaties in the catalogue of sources. Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists international conventions first, before custom and before general principles. And note the same structural point as in the introductory unit: paragraph d, judicial decisions and the teachings of publicists, is expressly labelled subsidiary means, and applies only, in the words of the article, subject to the provisions of Article 59.
slides.3: The sources, listed again, now as the map for this unit: treaties, international custom, general principles of law, decisions of international organizations, and unilateral acts. Set apart from those five are soft law and, separately, teachings and judicial decisions — set apart because they are not sources in the same sense. Treaties, the first item, are what the rest of this unit is about.
slides.4: No hierarchy of norms — except jus cogens. Two lines that decide a whole class of exam questions. There is no hierarchy among the sources, and the single exception is jus cogens. The standard examples of peremptory norms are the prohibitions of torture, apartheid, slavery and genocide. So if a treaty conflicts with custom, neither automatically wins on rank; but if either conflicts with a peremptory norm, the peremptory norm prevails.
slides.6: Decisions of international organizations, worked through on a real one: Security Council Resolution 1973 of 2011, on Libya. Two formulas in it matter. First, 'Determining that the situation continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security'. Second, 'Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter'. Those are the condition and the legal basis on which the Council may bind all states. The recitals also carry the responsibility-to-protect language about protecting the Libyan population.
slides.7: What a treaty looks like, across three millennia — five documents from wildly different worlds. The Treaty of Osnabrück, part of the Peace of Westphalia, 1648. The Austrian State Treaty of 1955. The Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, here dated 1296 BC and carved into a temple wall. And the Treaty of Lisbon of 2007. The point is the range: the form varies from a stone relief to a bound volume with wax seals, but the legal category is the same. And note a small discrepancy — this unit dates Kadesh to 1296 BC while the introductory unit said 1280 BC. The disagreement is in the sources, not in your notes.
slides.8: The twelve questions about a treaty. This is the structure of the whole unit, and the best case-solving checklist you will get. One, legal basis. Two, scope of application of the Vienna Convention. Three, treaty-making power. Four, adoption. Five, entry into force. Six, interpretation. Seven, scope of application. Eight, treaties and third states. Nine, modification. Ten, reservations. Eleven, invalidity. Twelve, termination and suspension. The list comes back throughout the unit with the current topic marked, so it doubles as your position marker. We start at item one, legal basis.
slides.10: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties: the dates that matter. The law of treaties is codified in the Convention of 1969 — and be careful, because 1969 is the date of adoption, not of entry into force. It entered into force only in 1980. Austria acceded in 1979, before entry into force. As of 2023 there are one hundred and sixteen parties, which is well short of the United Nations' one hundred and ninety-three members. That gap is the reason for what comes next.
slides.11: Who is party to the Vienna Convention. Parties cover most of Europe, much of Africa and much of South America. Signatories that have never ratified include, conspicuously, the United States and Iran. And outright non-parties include France, India, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey, among others. The lesson is practical: in a case involving a non-party or a mere signatory you cannot simply apply the Convention as a convention. You fall back on customary law.
slides.12: Back to the checklist, at item two: the scope of application of the Vienna Convention — the question whether the Convention applies at all to the agreement in front of you.
slides.13: When the Convention itself applies. The general definition of a treaty is wider than the Convention's own reach. For the Convention to apply as a convention, the agreement must be concluded between states — not with an international organization — and it must be in written form. Where those conditions fail, the agreement is still a treaty; it is simply governed by customary international law instead. In practice the two sets of rules largely coincide, because most of the Convention codifies custom.
slides.14: Bilateral and multilateral treaties. Picture two circles joined by a single double-headed arrow, and beside it five circles each joined to all the others. That contrast is the practical difference. In a bilateral treaty there is one relationship, so a breach or a reservation concerns one partner. In a multilateral treaty each party stands in a relationship with every other — which is why reservations, modification between some parties only, and termination all become complicated. Those are items nine to twelve on the checklist.
slides.15: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648, seen as treaty practice. Here is the detail the introductory unit left out: the peace was made in two places at once because of confession. Osnabrück was the Protestant venue, where the Holy Roman Empire settled with Sweden. Münster was the Catholic one, where Spain settled with the Netherlands, and the Empire with France. Two parallel congresses producing linked treaties — an early example of multilateral treaty-making by conference.
slides.16: The Congress of Vienna, 1814 and 1815. For the law of treaties the Congress matters as the model of the multilateral peace conference: many states negotiating one instrument together, rather than a web of bilateral settlements. That is the whole point being made; the material itself carries no further explanation.
slides.17: Self-executing and non-self-executing treaties — the second classification. It asks whether a provision can be applied by domestic authorities as it stands, or whether it first needs implementing legislation. The non-self-executing type is illustrated with Article 86 of the Rome Statute: 'States Parties shall cooperate fully with the Court in its investigation and prosecution of crimes'. That is an obligation addressed to the state, which must set up its own procedures before anything happens in a domestic courtroom. A self-executing provision, by contrast, is precise enough for a court or an official to apply directly.
slides.18: Checklist, item three: treaty-making power — who may bind the state.
slides.19: Treaty-making power, in three connected propositions. First, subjects of international law themselves stipulate which of their organs may conclude a treaty; international law does not prescribe it. Second, a person may act either on production of full powers, or in virtue of their functions — that is, by holding an office that carries the authority without a document. Third, if a treaty is concluded without full powers, it is either confirmed by retroactive consent, or it is invalid.
slides.22: Cameroon versus Nigeria, and Article 46 of the Vienna Convention — the standard case on what happens when a Head of State binds the state contrary to domestic constitutional rules. The judgment is the Land and Maritime Boundary case of 2002. The rule is in Article 46, paragraph 1: a state may not invoke the fact that its consent was expressed in violation of its internal law on competence to conclude treaties — unless that violation was manifest and concerned a rule of internal law of fundamental importance. Paragraph 2 then defines manifest: objectively evident to any state conducting itself in the matter in accordance with normal practice and in good faith. And the Court's conclusion: a limitation on a Head of State's capacity is not manifest unless it has at least been properly publicized.
slides.26: Checklist, item four: the adoption of a treaty — how a treaty text comes into being, and how a state becomes bound by it.
slides.29: Treaties requiring ratification: five stages. The long route adds two steps to the short one. Negotiations. Optional initialling. Signature. Domestic approval. And finally ratification. The state is bound only from ratification — signature alone does not bind on this route. But the stretch between signature and ratification is not empty: it carries the prohibition on defeating the object and purpose of the treaty. A signatory must not frustrate the treaty in the meantime, even though it is not yet bound by its substance. That interim duty is Article 18 of the Vienna Convention, and it is a favourite exam trap.
slides.34: The Erfüllungsvorbehalt — approval with a reservation of implementation, and this is the one with a real doctrinal point. When approving the racial discrimination convention, the Austrian National Council resolved, under Article 50, paragraph 2 of the Federal Constitution, that it was to be fulfilled by enacting laws. That is the Erfüllungsvorbehalt: parliament approves the treaty but declares that it will not be directly applicable, so courts and authorities cannot apply it until implementing legislation exists. It is the Austrian counterpart of the self-executing and non-self-executing distinction from earlier in this unit. Internationally, the treaty entered into force for Austria on the eighth of June 1972 regardless.
slides.35: The four ways of expressing consent to be bound. Signature, where no ratification is required. Ratification, defined here as the internal act of approval plus the declaration of acceptance. Accession. And exchange of instruments constituting a treaty. Note that composite definition of ratification — it has a domestic half and an international half, which is exactly what the Austrian example just showed.
slides.36: Checklist, item five: entry into force.
slides.39: Objective and subjective entry into force. Compare four treaties along the same rows — the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the Law of the Sea Convention, the Convention against Torture, and the Paris Agreement — and one distinction comes out of it. Objective entry into force is the date the treaty comes into force at all, once the required number of ratifications is reached: thirty-five, sixty, twenty and fifty-five respectively. Subjective entry into force is the date it comes into force for one particular state. A state that ratified early waits for the threshold: Austria ratified the Vienna Convention on the thirtieth of April 1979, but was bound only from the twenty-seventh of January 1980. A state that joins later waits only its own stipulated period: Switzerland deposited in 1990 and was bound thirty days after. In a case, always answer both questions separately.
slides.41: What entry into force triggers. The consequences split in two. On the timing side: the treaty applies from the agreed moment, or, if nothing was agreed, from consent by all negotiating parties. On the validity side, two rules to memorise. Article 26 of the Vienna Convention, pacta sunt servanda: every treaty in force binds the parties and must be performed in good faith. And Article 27: a party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform. The exception is the one from Cameroon versus Nigeria — a manifest violation of a rule of internal law of fundamental importance regarding competence, which is Articles 27 and 46 read together.
slides.42: Checklist, item six: interpretation — how the text of a treaty is to be read.
slides.43: Who interprets a treaty. Before the method comes the question of the interpreter, and the default answer is uncomfortable: interpretation is decentralized, meaning each party interprets for itself. Some treaties fix that by creating an organ competent to interpret, or by sending disputes to a court or arbitral tribunal. Two examples. Article 32 of the European Convention on Human Rights gives the European Court of Human Rights jurisdiction over all matters concerning interpretation and application of the Convention. And Article 1 of the Optional Protocol to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations puts such disputes under the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice.
slides.45: Interpretation, laid out as three branches. Ordinary meaning stands on its own. Systematic interpretation splits in two: Article 31, paragraph 2 — the treaty text with its preamble and attachments, plus every agreement or document made by the parties on the occasion of the conclusion; and Article 31, paragraph 3 — subsequent agreements, uniform subsequent practice by all the parties, and any relevant rules of international law between them, with Article 103 of the United Nations Charter as the example. And teleological interpretation carries effet utile and implied powers — implied powers mattering especially for international organizations.
slides.47: Article 36, paragraph 1, subparagraph b of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations — the provision being interpreted. The text: if a detained foreign national so requests, the authorities of the receiving state must without delay inform the consular post of the sending state; must forward any communication from the detainee to the consulate; and — these are the words that matter — must inform the person concerned without delay of his rights under the subparagraph. That last phrase is why the provision is famous. Read together with the preamble and the object and purpose, it was held to give rights to the individual, and not only to the sending state. That is what the LaGrand and Avena litigation before the International Court of Justice turned on.
slides.48: Checklist, item seven: scope of application. It branches into two questions that must be asked separately — the temporal scope, from when and until when does the treaty apply; and the territorial scope, to which territories.
slides.51: Checklist, item eight: treaties and third states.
slides.53: Checklist, item nine: modification of treaties. It branches into three words the lecture keeps apart — revision, amendment, and modification.
slides.54: Checklist, item ten: reservations. And one figure worth holding: across a series of human rights treaties, the percentage of state parties with at least one reservation runs from roughly a tenth to over half. Which is the point — reservations are not an exception, they are ordinary practice in multilateral treaty-making.
slides.59: The legal effect of a reservation: four possible reactions. This is the heart of the reservations topic — learn it as a decision tree. A reservation can be met with explicit acceptance, Article 20, paragraph 4, subparagraph a; or with tacit acceptance, Article 20, paragraph 5, which is silence for twelve months. Both create treaty relations between the accepting and the reserving state, with the provisions modified to the extent of the reservation, under Article 21. Or the reservation can be met with an objection — and everything then turns on the objection's form. An unqualified objection does not intend to preclude entry into force: the treaty applies between the two states, but under Article 21, paragraph 3 the provision to which the reservation relates does not apply between them, to the extent of the reservation. A qualified objection does preclude entry into force: under Article 20, paragraph 4, subparagraph b there are no treaty relations between those two states at all.
slides.61: Checklist, item eleven: invalidity of treaties. It branches into two questions to keep apart — the grounds of invalidity, and the procedure for invoking it.
slides.62: Invalidity for lack of consent. The first family of grounds concerns defects in who consented. One is the manifest violation of a rule of domestic law of fundamental importance — Article 46, which we met in Cameroon versus Nigeria. The other is acts of a person lacking competence to represent the state, and that splits in two: violation of internal law governing competence, and failure to observe a restriction on the representative's authority. Note the condition on that second one, and it carries an exclamation mark in the material: notification is needed. The restriction can only be invoked if it was notified to the other negotiating states beforehand.
slides.63: The other grounds of invalidity — five more, in ascending order of gravity. Error, meaning a mistaken impression of facts that vitiates consent. Fraud and corruption. Coercion of a representative of a state. Coercion of a state by the threat or use of force. And incompatibility with jus cogens. The illustration is a photograph of Emil Hácha with Hitler and Göring in Berlin in 1939 — the textbook case of coercion of a representative, the night the Czechoslovak president was pressed into signing away what remained of his state. And note the difference between the third ground and the fourth: coercion of the person, as against coercion of the state itself.
slides.64: Checklist, item twelve: termination and suspension — the last question on the list.
slides.65: Termination and suspension. Obligations can stop in two ways, and the difference reduces to one word each: termination is final, suspension is temporary. Everything that follows — the grounds, the procedure — attaches to one or the other. So in a case, always say which of the two is being claimed.
slides.66: Termination in bilateral and multilateral treaties: the same event has different names depending on the treaty. In a bilateral treaty, one party's exit ends the treaty — that is termination. In a multilateral treaty, one party's exit is withdrawal, and the treaty continues among the rest. This follows directly from the earlier picture: a bilateral treaty is one relationship, a multilateral treaty is many.
slides.70: The checklist, closed. All twelve questions have now been worked through. Use it as the skeleton for any treaty problem: legal basis; scope of the Vienna Convention; treaty-making power; adoption; entry into force; interpretation; scope of application; third states; modification; reservations; invalidity; termination.

outro: That is the end of Unit two. If you remember nothing else, remember the twelve questions — legal basis, scope of the Convention, treaty-making power, adoption, entry into force, interpretation, scope of application, third states, modification, reservations, invalidity, termination. Any treaty problem answers to that list.
